title: George IV
description: King of the United Kingdom from 1820 to 1830
wiki_lead:
George IV (George Augustus Frederick; 12 August 1762 – 26 June 1830) was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and King of Hanover from 29 January 1820 until his death in 1830. At the time of his accession to the throne, he was acting as prince regent for his father, King George III, having done so since 5 February 1811 during his father's final mental illness.
George IV was the eldest child of King George III and Queen Charlotte. Known affectionately as "Prinny" by friends, he led an extravagant lifestyle that contributed to the fashions of the Regency era. He was a patron of new forms of leisure, style and taste. He commissioned John Nash to build the Royal Pavilion in Brighton and remodel Buckingham Palace, and commissioned Jeffry Wyatville to rebuild Windsor Castle. George's charm and culture earned him the title "the first gentleman of England", but his dissolute way of life and poor relationships with his parents and his wife, Caroline of Brunswick, earned him the contempt of the people and dimmed the prestige of the monarchy. He excluded Caroline from his coronation and asked the government to introduce the unpopular Pains and Penalties Bill in an unsuccessful attempt to divorce her.
George's rule was tarnished by scandal and financial extravagance. His ministers found his behaviour selfish, unreliable and irresponsible, and he was strongly influenced by favourites. During most of George's regency and reign, Lord Liverpool controlled the government as prime minister of the United Kingdom. Liverpool's government presided over Britain's ultimate victory over Napoleon and negotiated a peace settlement with the French. After Liverpool's retirement, George was forced to accept Catholic emancipation despite opposing it. His only legitimate child, Princess Charlotte, predeceased him in 1817, as did his childless younger brother Prince Frederick in 1827, so he was succeeded by another younger brother, William IV.

Early life

George was born on 12 August 1762 at St James's Palace, London, the first child of King George III and Queen Charlotte. As the eldest son of a British sovereign, he automatically became Duke of Cornwall and Duke of Rothesay at birth; he was created Prince of Wales and Earl of Chester a few days later. George was baptised on 18 September by Thomas Secker, Archbishop of Canterbury. His godparents were his maternal uncle Adolphus Frederick IV, Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz (for whom the Lord Chamberlain, William Cavendish, 4th Duke of Devonshire, stood proxy); his paternal grand-uncle Prince William, Duke of Cumberland; and his grandmother Augusta, Dowager Princess of Wales.
George was a talented student and quickly learned to speak French, German and Italian, in addition to his native English.

grok_lead: George IV (George Augustus Frederick; 12 August 1762 â 26 June 1830) was King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and King of Hanover from 29 January 1820 until his death. As the eldest son of George III and Queen Charlotte, he served as Prince Regent from 1811 amid his father's recurrent mental instability, effectively wielding royal authority during a period of war with France and domestic unrest. George IV's tenure defined the Regency era's cultural splendor but was marred by personal excesses, including chronic indebtedness from lavish expenditures on palaces, art collections, and entertainments; multiple extramarital affairs, notably a clandestine marriage to Maria Fitzherbert invalidated by Catholic emancipation laws; and a notoriously acrimonious union with Caroline of Brunswick, culminating in a failed 1820 parliamentary bill to dissolve the marriage on grounds of her alleged adultery. His obesity, reliance on laudanum, and perceived frivolity fueled widespread ridicule, rendering him a figure of national derision despite contributions to architecture such as the Royal Pavilion at Brighton and support for neoclassical designs in London. Politically, his reign witnessed the Peterloo Massacre's aftermath, Catholic Relief Act of 1829, and early stirrings of reform, though his interventions often prioritized personal vendettas over principled governance.
